title: Political notes: Black Caucus looks back, ahead; giving a chance to vote, giving a test in Spanish
summary: In political notes, the Legislative Black Caucus has come a long way, but still has work ahead of it; former inmates can vote, if they know about it; and a test in another language is injusta.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 28, 2025

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 28, 2025

On the last day of Black History Month, Maryland state senators paused to highlight accomplishments and to look at what still needs to be done.

“We look around today, and we look at what’s going on on Capitol Hill. If there was ever a time that we need the Maryland Legislative Black office, it is now,” said  Sen. Joanne C. Benson (D-Prince George’s). “There is an attempt to turn back the clock for Black Americans.”

When Benson served as chair of the Legislative Black Caucus of Maryland in 1991, the caucus had no office and most of the state’s Black elected officials were concentrated in Prince George’s County and Baltimore City. Today, the 65-member delegation, just under 35% of the legislature, has an office on the third floor of the House office building. The 16 senators and 49 delegates in the caucus represent slightly more than 2 million Marylanders.

In the Senate, caucus members in major roles include Sen. Malcolm Augustine (D-Prince George’s) as Senate president pro tem; Sen. William C. Smith Jr. (D-Montgomery), chair of the Judicial Proceedings Committee, and Sen. Antonio Hayes (D-Baltimore City), the vice chair of the Finance Committee. In the House, caucus members in power roles start with Speaker Adrienne Jones (D-Baltimore County), the first Black delegate and first woman in the position, and include the majority whip and several committee chairs and vice chairs.

“As someone who went to law school, you’re raised to understand that there’s a rule of law … There are processes. He’s [Trump] destroying all of those norms,” Sydnor said. “While it makes it difficult, I think we’re here to say, ‘We’re that guardrail.’ We’re going to protect Marylanders as best we can.”

Benson had a direct message for businesses.

“If we have businesses in Prince George’s county and in the state of Maryland that are attempting to turn back the clock for us, they won’t last. That we can promise you,” she said.

Individuals released from state prison are allowed to apply for the right to vote it Maryland — but it’s mainly on them to figure it out.

When someone loses the right to vote because of a conviction “we sort of turn the lights off” on them, Del. Jheanelle Wilkins (D-Montgomery) said Monday. “We cancel, for all intents and purposes, their voter registration.”

Wilkins was testifying before the House Ways and Means Committee, which she co-chairs, as sponsor of a bill that would require the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services to electronically transmit names of those released from prison to the state Board of Elections. Under House Bill 1110, tbe department would send the board names of those eligible to vote every week, listing anyone released in the preceding week.

The board would have to identify each person on the department’s list who was registered to vote in Maryland before being incarcerated and has a new address in state. More importantly, the bill would “automatically restore the voter registration of each individual identified … and give the individual active voter status.”

Although eligible returning citizens are provided with voter information and even a voter registration card before their release, Joanne Antoine said some people don’t realize they can actually register to vote again.

“Imagine you coming home from a correctional facility right now, registering to vote is not top of mind. You’re thinking about your home, finding a job and so forth,” Antoine, executive director of Common Cause Maryland, said in an interview Monday after she testified in support of the bill.

“What we’re doing is creating a seamless process that will have a significant impact,” she said. “What we’re going to do is be able to register a ton of folks, and not just Black and brown. These are white folks. These are Republicans and so forth, who will be able to vote in our next election without any hurdles.”

The House on Friday advanced a bill to let individuals take the General Educational Development, better known as the GED, tests in either English or Spanish, over the objections of Republicans who said it would “dumb down” the test that is considered a stand-in for a high school diploma.

Before Friday’s 98-32 vote, Del. Lauren Arikan (R-Harford) said those who can speak several languages “are brilliant people.” But, “What we’re selling them with this is a lie. … Telling the child you will succeed in Maryland in the United States if you can’t take a test in English is a lie.”

That was echoed by Del. Kathy Szeliga (R-Baltimore County), who said she values foreign languages and speaks “a little Spanish myself, but I find this to be the dumbing down of the GED diploma. English is the international language of commerce and trade.” Szeliga said a GED “tells employers and those who receive it that they are either college- or career-ready. You are not college-ready if you cannot take a GED in English, and you are not career-ready, either. English unites us as a nation.”

Trump to sign executive order declaring English as official U.S. language

Supporters were having none of it.

Del. Deni Taveras (D-Prince George’s), a Dominican American, cited statistics that show the U.S. Latino economy grew from $3.2 trillion in 2021 to $3.6 trillion in 2022, and Spanish-speaking workers “have the right to be employed. They have the right to be educated,” she said. Del. Ashanti Martinez (D-Prince George’s), who chairs the Latino Caucus,, said many Latinos aren’t passing the GED tests, denying them a chance to participate in the economy.

“These are people with desire to participate in our economy,” Martinez said. “We talk a lot about making Maryland win the decade. If that’s going to happen, that means we have to use every single person to have pathways to opportunity for all of us.”

The state Labor Depatment, which administers GED tests, said 9,131 people whose primary language was Spanish enrolled in programs it offered in 2023-24. Of those individuals, 4,177, or 46%, did not have a high school diploma.

Del. Greg Wims (D-Montgomery), the bill’s sponsor, said after Friday’s vote that the measure is about “economic development.”

“Every student that gets his GED can either go into the military, go to college, get a job or start their own company,” he said. “From the very beginning, it was all about economic empowerment for those who don’t have the GED.”

If the bill passes, he said, Maryland would become the last state to give people the choice of taking the tests in English or Spanish. House Bill 325 now goes to the Senate, which gave unanimous approval Thursday to its own version of the bill.
